selected_news.source_headline: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
selected_news.article_text: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world” Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail) Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme) Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.” The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave” Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit? Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.” On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working? In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week? I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe? The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.” But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about? The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026 “There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?” Tuesday | The former health and social care secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield “PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison” The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply” Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade? This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. selected_news.title: COP31'de Türkiye, insan hakları baskısını durdurmalı
selected_news.summary: COP31 Explained: Why the Türkiye Climate Summit Matters Amnesty International USA
selected_news.source_headline: COP31 Explained: Why the Türkiye Climate Summit Matters
selected_news.article_text: November 16, 2026 | by Amnesty International From November 9 to 20, governments, scientists, activists, corporate lobbyists, diplomats, Indigenous Peoples and communities affected by climate change will gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for COP31, the annual UN climate conference COP31 comes after a year in which the climate crisis has become even harder to ignore. In September 2026, the United Nations acknowledged for the first time that the world is set to overshoot its target of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels within the next few years. The warning came as global temperatures continued to soar, with the last two months setting global heat records The science is undeniable; the legal obligations irrefutable; and the human rights stakes unfathomable. Human activities, particularly the extraction and burning of coal, oil and gas, are heating the planet and intensifying threats to human rights. Governments cannot portray climate inaction as a neutral position. Climate inaction, and worse, governmental provision of tax, political, and regulatory support to the fossil fuel industry, are deliberate choices made in the face of overwhelming evidence, with devastating consequences for people and their rights. By acting together and placing justice at the center of climate action, governments can still limit further harm and build a fairer future COP stands for Conference of the Parties. It is the main decision-making forum of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, or UNFCCC, the international treaty agreed in 1992 and the parent treaty of the 2015 Paris Agreement COP meetings bring almost every country together to negotiate collective action, based on historical responsibility and capacity, on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, adapting to climate change and supporting countries and communities experiencing loss and damage This year’s unusual leadership arrangement gives both Türkiye and Australia significant responsibility as co-hosts. Türkiye will host COP31 and Australia will lead the official negotiations. Both countries must demonstrate credible climate leadership and not hide behind each other to deflect attention from their lack of action. Türkiye’s continuing reliance on coal and pursuit of fossil gas risk locking it into a high-emissions pathway. Australia must confront the contradiction between leading global climate negotiations and continuing to support fossil fuel extraction and use Official pre-COP meetings and leaders’ events already took place in Fiji and Tuvalu from October 5 to 8, bringing Pacific leadership and priorities into the run-up to the main summit. Amnesty International has documented how climate change is already harming human rights in Tuvalu, Kiribati and other Pacific Island countries. In Tuvalu, Kiribati and across the region, rising seas, extreme heat, drought and saltwater intrusion threaten people’s rights to water, food, health, housing, culture and a safe future Students from the Pacific took the fight against climate change to the world’s top court, leading the International Court of Justice to issue a landmark Advisory Opinion in July 2025, which made it clear that governments have a legal obligation to protect human rights from climate change impacts After more than 30 years of climate negotiations, governments can no longer hide behind promises of future action. The science is settled, the solutions are available and the resources exist. Continued delay is a political choice, one that protects fossil fuel interests while Pacific communities lose land, livelihoods, rights and cultural heritage As President of Negotiations, Australia must ensure that Pacific demands become concrete COP31 outcomes. It cannot credibly claim climate leadership abroad while expanding fossil fuel projects at home that deepen the harms to Indigenous People, Pacific neighbors, and other frontline communities. Australia must end this contradiction by ending fossil fuel expansion, accelerating a just transition and securing far greater support for communities facing irreversible loss and damage Every COP matters, but the window for preventing escalating and irreversible harm is closing rapidly. In October 2026, the UN Environment Program warned that the world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. The higher and longer the overshoot, the greater the danger to people, ecosystems and economies. The harm caused cannot be undone Overshooting 1.5°C cannot become an excuse for resignation. Every fraction of a degree matters to human and planetary life. Governments must cut emissions urgently through a just and equitable phase out of fossil fuels, protect affected communities and prevent warming from reaching even more dangerous levels Yet many major economies continue to approve new fossil fuel production and prolong dependence on coal, oil and gas, including through subsidies, tax breaks, and other support. In many contexts, the fossil fuel industry is a powerful actor, shaping politics and legislation domestically and overseas. Meanwhile, climate science is being undermined and the social solidarity needed to drive action is being deliberately fractured by authoritarian state and corporate forces. The result is a vicious cycle of disinformation, regulatory sabotage, coercive diplomacy and fossil fuel lock-in. It lays bare a widening gap between what science tells us is necessary and what human rights law obligates governments to do one hand, and what governments are willing to do on the other hand Everyone has the right to live in a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. Climate change also threatens the rights to life, food, water, health, housing, culture and an adequate standard of living In 2026, unprecedented climate-related disasters worldwide and their human consequences were visible across the world The human cost of climate breakdown is impossible to ignore any longer We know that humans’ burning of fossil fuels is the main source of greenhouse gases that become concentrated in our atmosphere. These gases trap the sun’s heat, leading to a long-term rise in the planet’s average temperature and causing shifts in weather patterns as well as rising sea levels that will wipe out small island states and much low-lying coastal land Therefore, to protect human rights now and in the future and prevent even greater harm, governments must deliver a full, fast, fair and funded phase-out of fossil fuels There are many alternatives to fossil fuels, like wind and solar power, that will enable us to reduce our dependency on fossil fuels. The global push towards electrification using renewable energy is essential, but the transition must respect human rights and not reproduce the abuses and inequalities of the fossil fuel economy Amnesty International is calling on governments to advance three priorities Justice demands that those most responsible for heating the planet, and those with the greatest capacity to act, do and pay their fair share In September, the Turkish authorities launched a nationwide operation targeting LGBTI+ organizations, activists and human rights defenders. Homes, venues and offices were raided, more than 100 people were detained, dozens of whom were subsequently remanded in pretrial detention and over 1000 social media accounts belonging to activists, journalists and human rights organizations were blocked or restricted, including that of Amnesty International Türkiye. In October, in another serious escalation, authorities raided and seized control of a major opposition television channel in a significant blow to press freedom This is not an isolated attack or one confined to a single community. It is part of a sustained crackdown with arbitrary restrictions on peaceful assembly, association and expression over the last decade. Environmental defenders, journalists, women’s rights activists, political opponents and LGBTI+ communities may be targeted in different ways, but the effect is the same: dissent is silenced, divisions are stoked, and fear spreads – making it harder for people to hold their government accountable for climate action or any other human rights issue For the vital negotiations about protecting our shared future to be effective and equitable at COP31, Türkiye must end its crackdown on human rights and those who defend them UN climate conferences remain among the few global spaces where almost all states come together alongside Indigenous Peoples, civil society representatives in all their diversity and communities campaigning for climate justice. Fossil fuel lobbyists will be there too – as they are in almost all forums where climate change is discussed. Protecting civic space at COP is essential to overcoming fossil fuel obstruction and securing effective climate action. As it is, the scales are tipped in favor of industry. Any erosion in protections for civil society at COP will tip the scales further Around the world, governments and corporations have criminalized protest and subjected environmental human rights defenders to intimidation, surveillance, detention and violence. Authoritarian attacks on environmental human rights defenders, women, LGBTI+ people and other marginalized communities are not separate political projects. They divide societies, weaken collective action and protect entrenched power while fossil fuel production continues Yet people continue to resist as documented by Amnesty International in its new briefing, ‘Protecting our Future: Environmental Human Rights Defenders Powering Just Transitions’ There can be no climate justice without the freedom to demand it
